The Blue antimora (Antimora rostrata) is a bathyal fish whose life history is shaped by the deep ocean environment. At a habitat temperature of 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is estimated at 40 years [am = 40 years], although the oldest individual precisely aged through otolith analysis reached 38 years, suggesting that the true longevity may be slightly greater. This species attains a maximum reported total length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters], representing the largest individuals captured in longline surveys across the North Atlantic. The neonatal wet weight derived from the average egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters is approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a minuscule starting mass that underscores the extreme fecundity necessary for population persistence in the deep sea. Females in this species reach the onset of puberty at a total length of 42 centimeters [Lp = 42 centimeters], as determined from macroscopic examination of gonadal development in trawl-caught specimens. This length at maturity corresponds to an age of approximately 19 to 20 years according to published growth models, indicating a remarkably delayed reproductive schedule consistent with the slow pace of life in cold, food-limited environments.

Reproductive output in Antimora rostrata reflects a strategy of high fecundity coupled with small offspring size. Under the stable thermal regime of the deep ocean at 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C], individual females are capable of a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 2,466 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,466 eggs per day], derived from potential fecundity estimates and the assumption of annual spawning periodicity. The vast numerical investment in minute pelagic eggs, each measuring roughly 0.8 millimeters in diameter, is a classic adaptation for species that release offspring into an environment where early-stage mortality is extraordinarily high. The resulting wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] is among the lowest recorded for teleosts of comparable adult size, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a cold, resource-poor habitat. This high-fecundity, low-per-offspring-investment model is typical of many deep-sea fishes, where the probability of a single larva surviving to recruitment is infinitesimally small.

The growth trajectory of Antimora rostrata is extremely protracted, a consequence of the low metabolic demand at the ambient temperature of 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C] and the sparse food availability on the continental slope. The species reaches an ultimate total length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters] only after many decades of slow somatic expansion, with von Bertalanffy growth parameters indicating a very low growth coefficient. This pattern of delayed maturation is exemplified by the length at which females attain puberty, recorded at 42 centimeters [Lp = 42 centimeters], which corresponds to about half the maximum length but requires roughly two decades to achieve. The physiological underpinnings of this strategy involve the allocation of energy primarily to maintenance and slow structural growth rather than to early reproduction. Comparative studies with other morids, such as Antimora microlepis, show a similar life-history syndrome, although Antimora rostrata occupies a slightly shallower depth range on average. The ultimate body size of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters] places it among the larger members of its genus, with implications for its trophic role as a benthopelagic predator.

Detailed investigations into the reproductive biology of the Blue antimora have clarified the relationship between body size and the onset of sexual maturation. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from a size-stratified sample confirmed that 50 percent of females are mature at a total length of 42 centimeters [Lp = 42 centimeters], a figure consistent with earlier macroscopic assessments. This size threshold appears to be critical for initiating vitellogenesis and the subsequent production of the large number of small, pelagic oocytes characteristic of the species. The estimated lifespan of 40 years [am = 40 years] provides a long window for repeated spawning events, though the frequency of reproduction in any given year remains poorly understood for wild populations at a temperature of 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C]. At the prevailing deep-sea temperature of 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C], metabolic rates are suppressed, which likely contributes to the extended time required to reach sexual maturity and the slow accumulation of reproductive biomass. Further research is needed to determine whether individual females spawn annually or at longer intervals, as seen in many other deep-water gadiforms.

Longevity data for Antimora rostrata, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated otolith readings, suggest a maximum attainable age of around 40 years [am = around 40 years] under natural conditions at the typical thermal regime of 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C]. This lifespan is substantial for a teleost of its size and is comparable to that of some deep-sea rockfishes (Sebastes spp.) that inhabit similar thermal niches. The ultimate total length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters] likely represents the maximum size that can be supported by the available prey biomass and the metabolic constraints of the environment. The very high fecundity, expressed as approximately 2,466 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,466 eggs per day], is necessary to offset the immense mortality experienced during the long pelagic larval and juvenile phases. These life-history traits—extreme longevity, late maturity, enormous fecundity, and minute offspring—collectively define a conservative, bet-hedging strategy that is exquisitely tuned to the stable but unproductive deep-sea ecosystem that Antimora rostrata inhabits.
